#### Plot Fonts and Theme

```{r}
#| label: plot-theme
#| echo: true
#| cache: false
#| code-fold: true
#| messages: false
#| warning: false

library(systemfonts)
library(showtext)
## Clean the slate
systemfonts::clear_local_fonts()
systemfonts::clear_registry()
##
showtext_opts(dpi = 96) #set DPI for showtext
sysfonts::font_add(family = "Alegreya",
  regular = "../../../../../../fonts/Alegreya-Regular.ttf",
  bold = "../../../../../../fonts/Alegreya-Bold.ttf",
  italic = "../../../../../../fonts/Alegreya-Italic.ttf",
  bolditalic = "../../../../../../fonts/Alegreya-BoldItalic.ttf")

sysfonts::font_add(family = "Roboto Condensed", 
  regular = "../../../../../../fonts/RobotoCondensed-Regular.ttf",
  bold = "../../../../../../fonts/RobotoCondensed-Bold.ttf",
  italic = "../../../../../../fonts/RobotoCondensed-Italic.ttf",
  bolditalic = "../../../../../../fonts/RobotoCondensed-BoldItalic.ttf")
showtext_auto(enable = TRUE) #enable showtext
##
theme_custom <- function(){ 
    font <- "Alegreya"   #assign font family up front
    
    theme_classic(base_size = 14, base_family = font) %+replace%    #replace elements we want to change
    
    theme(
      text = element_text(family = font),  #set base font family
      
      #text elements
      plot.title = element_text(                 #title
                   family = font,          #set font family
                   size = 24,                    #set font size
                   face = 'bold',                #bold typeface
                   hjust = 0,                    #left align
                   margin = margin(t = 5, r = 0, b = 5, l = 0)), #margin
      plot.title.position = "plot", 
      
      plot.subtitle = element_text(              #subtitle
                   family = font,          #font family
                   size = 14,                   #font size
                   hjust = 0,                   #left align
                   margin = margin(t = 5, r = 0, b = 10, l = 0)), #margin
      
      plot.caption = element_text(               #caption
                   family = font,          #font family
                   size = 9,                     #font size
                   hjust = 1),                   #right align
      
      plot.caption.position = "plot",            #right align
      
      axis.title = element_text(                 #axis titles
                   family = "Roboto Condensed",  #font family
                   size = 12),                   #font size
      
      axis.text = element_text(                  #axis text
                   family = "Roboto Condensed",  #font family
                   size = 9),                    #font size
      
      axis.text.x = element_text(                #margin for axis text
                    margin = margin(5, b = 10))
      
      #since the legend often requires manual tweaking 
      #based on plot content, don't define it here
    )
}

## Use available fonts in ggplot text geoms too!
ggplot2::update_geom_defaults(geom = "text",new = list(
  family = "Roboto Condensed",
  face = "plain",
  size = 3.5,
  color = "#2b2b2b"
)
)
ggplot2::update_geom_defaults(geom = "label", new = list(
  family = "Roboto Condensed",
  face = "plain",
  size = 3.5,
  color = "#2b2b2b"
)
)

## Set the theme
ggplot2::theme_set(new = theme_custom())

```



## {{< iconify clarity group-solid >}} Bayes Rule: Do Exclamation Marks in Headlines help define fake news?


Let us replicate the initial analysis in Chapter 2 of the book *Bayes Rule* by Mine Dogucu et al. The goal is to update our beliefs about the probability of a coin being fair given new evidence.

Let us first define our events:

1. Event F: News item is *fake* or *real*. p = c(0.4, 0.6) for fake and real news, respectively. These are our ***prior*** probabilities.
2. Event E: News item has an exclamation mark in the headline. Looking at the ***data***, we find that :

```{r}
#| label: prior-probabilities
#| code-fold: true
data(fake_news, package = "bayesrules")
fake_news %>% glimpse()
fake_news %>% count(type)
fake_news %>% count(title_has_excl)
```
We can see that 60 out of 150 news items are fake, and 90 are real. Of the fake news, 16 have an exclamation mark in the title, while only 2 of the real news have an exclamation mark in the title.
We can summarize this information in a contingency table:

```{r}
#| label: likelihoods
#| code-fold: true
vcd::structable(type ~ title_has_excl, data = fake_news) %>% 
  addmargins()

```

And the ***likelihoods*** of the events are: 

- $P(E | F)$: Exclamation given Fake: 16/60 = 0.267
- $P(E | F_c)$: Exclamation given Real: 2/90 = 0.022
- $P(E_c | F )$: No Exclamation given Fake: 44/60 = 0.733
- $P(E_c | F_c)$: No Exclamation given Real: 88/90 = 0.978


Now we can use Bayes Rule to update our beliefs about the probability of a news item being fake given that it has an exclamation mark in the title: Here is the logic of that update:

1. We have $P(F) = 0.4$ and $P(F_c) = 0.6$
2. We have $P(E | F) = 0.267$ and $P(E | F_c) = 0.022$
3. We **want**: $P(F | E) = P(E | F) * P(F) / P(E) = ?$

Where P(E) is the total probability of E, which can be calculated as:

$$
P(E) = P(E | F) * P(F) + P(E | F_c) * P(F_c)
$$

4. We can calculate the ***posterior*** probability of a news item being fake given that it has an exclamation mark in the title using Bayes Rule:

```{r}
#| label: bayes-rule
#| code-fold: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

prior <- c(0.4, 0.6) # P(F) and P(F_c)
likelihood <- c(0.267, 0.022) # P(E | F) and P(E | F_c)
posterior <- likelihood * prior / 
  (likelihood[1] * prior[1] + likelihood[2] * prior[2])
posterior <- round(posterior, 3)
posterior
posterior_df <- tibble(
  type = c("Fake", "Real"),
  posterior = posterior
)
posterior_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = type, y = posterior, fill = type)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#d62728", "#1f77b4")) +
  labs(title = "Posterior Probability of Fake News",
       subtitle = "Given an Exclamation Mark in the Title",
       x = "News Type",
       y = "Posterior Probability") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```

So now we know how to compute the likelihoods and the posterior probabilities using Bayes Rule. Let us do this for a sequence of 10000 headlines, which we will generate by sampling the `fake_news` dataset with replacement. We will update our beliefs about the probability of a news item being fake as we get new evidence (i.e., as we see more headlines with or without exclamation marks).

## A Simulation

Let us simulate a run where we get a series of headlines and see how our beliefs about the probability of a news item being fake change as we get new evidence. We will use the `fake_news` dataset to simulate this process. We will sample from this dataset with replacement 10000 times ( as done in the text, and plot the posterior probabilities as we go along.)

We will create a function to compute the likelihood from each observation and update the posterior probability using Bayes Rule.  

```{r}
#| label: bayes-simulation-setup
#| code-fold: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false

prior <- c(0.4, 0.6) # P(F) and P(F_c)
# Define possible articles
article <- data.frame(type = c("real", "fake"))

# Simulate 10000 articles. 
set.seed(84735)
article_sim <- sample_n(article, size = 10000, 
                        weight = prior, replace = TRUE) %>% 
  mutate(data_model = case_when(type == "fake" ~ 0.2667,
                                type == "real" ~ 0.0222))

glimpse(article_sim)

```

```{r}
#| label: bayes-function
#| code-fold: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

bayes_update <- function(prior, likelihood, likelihood_c) {
  posterior <- likelihood * prior[1] / 
    (likelihood * prior[1] + likelihood_c * prior[2])
  posterior <- round(posterior, 3)
  prior <- posterior
  return(posterior)
}

```

Now let us run the simulation. We will simulate the usage of exclamation points in the headlines based on the data model we have defined. We will then update our beliefs about the probability of a news item being fake as we get new evidence.

```{r}
data <- c("no", "yes")

# Simulate exclamation point usage 
set.seed(3)
article_sim <- article_sim %>%
  group_by(1:n()) %>% 
  mutate(usage = sample(data, size = 1, 
                        prob = c(1 - data_model, data_model))) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  rename(id = `1:n()`)
article_sim
article_sim %>% group_by(type, usage) %>% count()

```


```{r}
article_sim %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = usage, fill = type)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") + # Proportion of usage
  labs(title = "Exclamation Point Usage in Headlines",
       x = "Usage",
       y = "Proportion") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#d62728", "#1f77b4")) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

ggplot(article_sim, aes(x = type)) + 
  geom_bar(aes(fill = type)) + 
  facet_wrap(~ usage) +   scale_fill_manual(values = c("#d62728", "#1f77b4"))

```

We now have a simulated dataset of 10000 articles with a type (fake or real) and an exclamation point usage (yes or no). We can now use this dataset to update our beliefs about the probability of a news item being fake given that it has an exclamation mark in the title.

Each time we update the posterior probability, we will store the result in a data frame. The posterior from the previous iteration becomes the prior for the next iteration.

```{r}
#| label: bayes-simulation
#| code-fold: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

posterior_df <- data.frame(
  iteration = integer(),
  fake = numeric(),
  real = numeric()
)
for (i in 1:nrow(article_sim)) {
  # Get the current article type and usage
  current_article <- article_sim[i, ]
  
  # Determine the likelihood based on the article type
  if (current_article$type == "fake") {
    likelihood <- 0.2667
    likelihood_c <- 0.7333
  } else {
    likelihood <- 0.0222
    likelihood_c <- 0.9778
  }
  
  # Update the posterior probability using Bayes Rule
  posterior <- bayes_update(prior, likelihood, likelihood_c)
  
  # Store the result in the data frame
  posterior_df <- rbind(posterior_df, 
                        data.frame(iteration = i, 
                                   fake = posterior[1], 
                                   real = posterior[2]))
    # Update the prior for the next iteration
  prior <- posterior
}
posterior_df
posterior_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = iteration)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fake, color = "Fake"), size = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = real, color = "Real"), size = 1) +
  labs(title = "Posterior Probability of Fake News",
       subtitle = "Updated with Each New Article",
       x = "Iteration",
       y = "Posterior Probability") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Fake" = "#d62728", "Real" = "#1f77b4")) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")






```
